Guide

How to read the options report

The options report ranks contracts that an option seller might study. This guide explains each column, why short-dated yields look enormous, and what the backtest does and does not show.

What the report is about

The report looks at two income strategies on a reviewed list of US stocks and ETFs. In a cash-secured put you sell a put and hold enough cash to buy the shares at the strike if they are assigned to you. In a covered call you sell a call against shares you already own. In both cases you are paid a premium now and accept an obligation later.

The seller's profit is capped at the premium. The loss is not capped in the same way: a put seller who is assigned owns shares bought at the strike, however far the market has fallen below it. Keep that asymmetry in mind for every number that follows.

The columns

Strike and distance

The strike is the price at which shares change hands if the option is exercised. Distance is how far the strike sits from the current share price, as a percentage. For a put, a strike 8% below the share price means the shares can fall 8% before the option is in the money. More distance means more room, and a smaller premium.

Premium

The premium is the bid price per share. One contract covers 100 shares, so a premium of $2.40 is $240 per contract before fees. The report only lists contracts with a bid between $1.00 and $7.00, which removes contracts too cheap to be worth the commission and contracts so expensive that they are already deep in the money.

Expiry and days

Days is the number of calendar days until the option expires. Short-dated options lose time value fastest, and they are also the most sensitive to a sudden move in the shares.

Implied volatility

Implied volatility (IV) is the volatility figure that makes an option-pricing model agree with the market price. It is quoted as an annual percentage. High IV means the market is pricing a wide range of outcomes, often because of earnings or news. High IV is the reason a premium is large, so a rich premium and a risky underlying usually arrive together.

Annualized yield

For a put this is the premium divided by the strike, scaled to a year:

annualized % = premium ÷ strike × 365 ÷ days × 100

This is the column most likely to mislead. A $2.40 premium on a $42 strike with three days to run is a 5.7% return on the cash set aside. Multiplying by 365 ÷ 3 gives about 695% a year. Nobody earns that, because it assumes the same trade can be repeated 121 times in a row without one assignment. Read annualized yield as a way to compare contracts of similar length, never as an expected return.

Probability out of the money

This is a model estimate, from the Black-Scholes formula using the contract's implied volatility, of the chance that the option expires worthless and the seller keeps the whole premium. A figure of 80% does not mean the trade is safe. It means the model expects the bad outcome about one time in five, and says nothing about how bad it is when it comes.

Composite score

The score puts four things on one 0 to 100 scale: yield, distance, delta and the speed of time decay. It deliberately discounts yields from contracts shorter than 30 days. The exact weights are in how DappGo computes its signals. The score ranks contracts against each other on the same day. It is not a probability and it has no meaning across days.

Reading the daily page

The archive page for each session starts with how many candidates passed the filters and how their expiries are distributed. A day on which most candidates expire within a week is a day when the list is dominated by fast, sensitive contracts. Next comes the highest-scored candidate for each underlying, then a breakdown of the score for the top rows, so you can see whether a high score came from yield or from distance. The implied-volatility table shows which underlyings the market expects to move most.

The backtest

Each page repeats the report's reference backtest with its dates. Look at two numbers together: the win rate and the profit factor. Option selling normally shows a high win rate, because most options expire worthless. The profit factor, total gains divided by total losses, tells you whether the wins paid for the losses. A win rate above 80% with a profit factor below 1 is a losing record. The backtest covers a short, fixed window and a small number of underlyings, so it describes that period only.

Before you act on anything

Check the earnings date of the underlying, the bid-ask spread in your own broker, and whether you are willing to own the shares at the strike. The report cannot do any of these for you. It is research material, not advice. The glossary defines the terms used here.
